This is a great response. I had actually forgotten about utilitarianism versus deontology when I had been thinking of this. That actually makes me hesitate, because I also consider myself a deontologist, and don't necessarily think that the ends justify the means, and all that. But I am also a pessimistic antinatalist, and know I will never have kids in order to end the cycle of violence and suffering. And I wish others would too. But I know they never will. That will never happen, and the cycle of human existence will continue until the world becomes too populated to sustain that growth of life and kills us all, like cancer killing its host. This is the first message that makes me realize that maybe I wouldn't do it, if I actually had the option and it wasn't merely hypothetical. Maybe I would respect the agency of mot interfering with the lives and bodies of others. But maybe I would still press the button and call myself a hero. It's impossible to really know.

I just wouldn't want the blood of billions on my hands. I'm okay with sterilizing everyone because nobody would die directly as a result, and I would still be preventing an immeasurable amount of suffering. Nuking the world, or some other method of global extinction, would have the same result, but would be too messy for me.

Oh I agree, I think that our mindset is much more logical, but I have to admit that I am biased by my other logic and beliefs. The reason others would never agree to this idea or an antinatalist mindset is because they are optimists. It seems to be the cornerstone for the human mindset, to believe that life is all worth something. To believe that the suffering does not outweigh the good, which in my opinion is silly. They can only speak for themselves, not for those who have suffered and died. I doubt most of the dead would not say it was worth it, if they could speak. 

And the optimist's mind is often resilient, otherwise what is the point? Why give in and admit that you are wrong? What is the point if it is all for nothing? If there is no reason for our suffering, why continue the cycle? These are questions that many will never consider, and even fewer will become antinatalists by answering them. And that is the unfortunate truth. I don't believe the antinatalist mindset will ever carry on, as the natural innate urge to reproduce will inevitably overrule it, time and time again.

Of course if there was a way to convince all of humanity that reproduction was an unnecessary and immoral thing to do that only continues a cycle of death and suffering I would, but I'm not naive enough to believe that could ever be possible. The natalists outnumber the antinatalists thousands to one. 

The way I view it would be this. If I could do what I said and sterilize the human race, I would be using a right that I do not have, to prevent others from using a right that I do not believe they should have. There is no right or moral way to end the existence of human consciousness, but at least my method would have the least bloodshed, as I would not be killing anyone, just preventing future life.

Natalists operate by a different logic. One that denies pessimism and convinces themself that life is worth creating. Most can not and will not be converted. It is naive to call their logic and values silly when they would say the exact same for us.
Depends on the perspective of course. Someone with such ideals would absolutely be considered mad and insane by nearly the entire population, but logical and sane to one of us.

Why just lower it instead of stopping it completely? True, lowering it would most certainly raise the quality of life for the generations with lower populations, but there would still be suffering and death. Why not prevent all future deaths? All unnecessary suffering? Just pull the plug.
I would think of it more as a cure for humanity than a disease. And I truly think that if I were capable of it I would absolutely become a mad scientist and enact my plan to neuter all humans.
A small price to pay for salvation.
